# Digest R1 — James 1:1–18
**Range:** raw L525–726 (cache file `R1-1_1-1_18.txt`, lines 1–200 of that file)
**Agent coverage:** Read full assigned cache file end-to-end (letter opening 1:1; structure of 1:2–18; trials 1:2–4; wisdom/double-mindedness 1:5–8; poor/rich 1:9–11; blessed endurance 1:12; temptation chain 1:13–15; good gifts / new birth 1:16–18). Brief glance at following transition to 1:19–2:26 only as Moo frames the close of 1:2–18. No outside knowledge. No wiki edits.

## Claims

### C-R1-001
- **Claim:** Letter openings are not mere formalities; James’s introduction describes writer and recipients in ways that give important clues about the letter’s nature and purposes.
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "Many readers skip the opening verses of NT letters, treating them as unimportant formal details. But this is a mistake. For the letter introductions usually contain more than bare names. They also describe the writer and the recipients in ways that provide us with important clues about the nature and purposes of the letter that follows."
- **Locus:** Jas 1:1 / letter introduction (cache L1)
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **Type:** interpretive

### C-R1-002
- **Claim:** Because James is writing a letter to a specific audience, he will move rapidly from topic to topic as he addresses their various needs and issues; accurate application depends on understanding what he said to the original readers.
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "We will expect, for instance, that James writes for a specific audience - the addressees of the letter - and that what he says will be largely determined by their situation and needs. This being the case, we will not be surprised if James moves rapidly from topic to topic as he takes up these various needs and issues."
- **Locus:** Jas 1:1 / letter genre and audience (cache L2)
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **Type:** interpretive

### C-R1-003
- **Claim:** James expands the ancient letter form only briefly: a short title for himself, a loaded though ambiguous theological phrase for the recipients, and the simple “greetings.”
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "James's expansions are much briefer. He adds only a brief title to his own name. Instead of identifying the recipients of his letter by name or place of residence, he describes them with a loaded, though ambiguous, theological phrase. And he retains the simple \"greetings\" of most ancient letters."
- **Locus:** Jas 1:1 / epistolary form (cache L3)
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **Type:** textual-observation

### C-R1-004
- **Claim:** The sender “James” is the Lord’s brother (Gal. 1:19; cf. Gal. 2:9, 12; 1 Cor. 15:7), leader of the early church in Jerusalem (Acts 12:17; 15:13; 21:18); pseudonymous authorship faces serious difficulties and the straightforward claim of the verse should be accepted.
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "\"James,\" as we argued in the Introduction, is the \"brother of the Lord\" mentioned by Paul in Gal. 1:19 (cf. also Gal. 2:9,12;1 Cor. 15:7), the James who was leader of the early church in Jerusalem (Acts 12:17; 15:13; 21:18). We have also noted that many contemporary scholars doubt that James himself is the author of the letter. They argue that someone else, perhaps in the latter years of the first century, wrote in his name. But this theory faces serious difficulties (see the Introduction for details). We should accept the straightforward claim of this verse: the best-known James in the early church, the Lord's brother, wrote this letter."
- **Locus:** Jas 1:1 / authorship (cache L9)
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, james-the-just, moo-james-pntc]
- **Type:** historical-position

### C-R1-005
- **Claim:** James does not mention his physical kinship to Jesus because that relationship gave him no authority to admonish other Christians; what qualified him was his spiritual relationship.
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "But if James the Lord's brother wrote this letter, why does he not mention his special relationship to Jesus? Probably because being a brother of Jesus gave James no authority to admonish other Christians as he does in this letter. What qualified James to write such a letter was not his physical relationship to Jesus but his spiritual relationship."
- **Locus:** Jas 1:1 / why no kinship claim (cache L11)
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, james-the-just, moo-james-pntc]
- **Type:** interpretive

### C-R1-006
- **Claim:** James was not one of the original twelve apostles, but like Paul may have been added after the resurrection; Gal. 1:19 suggests Paul at least viewed him as an apostle, yet James does not claim that status for himself.
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "James was not, of course, one of the original twelve apostles. But, like Paul, James might have been added to the ranks of the apostles after the resurrection. And Gal. 1:19 suggests that Paul, at least, viewed James as an apostle: \"I saw none of the other apostles - only James, the Lord's brother.\"' Nevertheless, James does not claim this status for himself."
- **Locus:** Jas 1:1 / apostolic status (cache L11–13)
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, james-the-just, moo-james-pntc]
- **Type:** interpretive

### C-R1-007
- **Claim:** By calling himself a “servant” (Gk. also “slave”), James acknowledges subservience, yet “servant of God” also carries great honor, applied in the OT to leaders such as Moses and David; like Paul and Peter, James uses a title that suggests authority to address and admonish.
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "He identifies himself simply as \"a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ.\" By calling himself a \"servant,\" James of course acknowledges his subservient status. Indeed, the Greek word translated \"servant\" in the NIV also means \"slave\" (see NLT). But being a \"servant of God\" - because it is God, the sovereign of the universe whom one serves - also carries great honor. For in the OT, this title is applied to the great leaders of the people of Israel, such as Moses (Deut. 34:5; Dan. 9:11) and David (Jer. 33:21; Ezek. 37:25). As do Paul (cf. Rom. 1:1; Gal. 1:10; Phil. 1:1; Tit. 1:1) and Peter (2 Pet. 1:1), James therefore identifies himself in the letter opening with a title that suggests his authority to address - and admonish - the readers."
- **Locus:** Jas 1:1 / “servant of God” (cache L13)
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, james-the-just, moo-james-pntc]
- **Type:** interpretive

### C-R1-008
- **Claim:** The full phrase “servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ” is unique in the NT; James does not mean both “God” and “Lord” apply to Jesus (order would then be opposite) but that he serves both God and “the Lord Jesus Christ.”
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "If the title \"servant of God\" is common, the full description \"servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ\" is not. Only here in the NT does this language occur. James could intend both titles, \"God\" and \"Lord,\" to apply to Jesus - \"Jesus Christ, both God and Lord.\"2 But we would have expected the titles to occur in the opposite order had this been James's intention. His point rather is that he serves both God and \"the Lord Jesus Christ.\""
- **Locus:** Jas 1:1 / servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ (cache L15)
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, james-the-just, moo-james-pntc]
- **Type:** interpretive

### C-R1-009
- **Claim:** “Christ” is a title equivalent to OT/Jewish “Messiah”; James’s addition of “Lord” reflects early Christian understanding (Acts 2:36), showing a transformation in James’s view of his half-brother Jesus.
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "We are so used to the combination \"Jesus Christ\" that we forget that \"Christ\" is a title, equivalent to the OT/Jewish \"Messiah.\" While rarely used in the OT, this title was beginning to be used in the NT period to denote the deliverer/king expected by Jews in the last days. James's addition of the title \"Lord\" reflects a very early Christian understanding of Jesus, as seen in Peter's claim in his Day-of-Pentecost sermon: \"God has made this Jesus, whom you crucified, both Lord and Christ\" (Acts 2:36). James's view of his half-brother Jesus had undergone quite a transformation since the days they grew up in the same household together!"
- **Locus:** Jas 1:1 / Christ / Lord (cache L15)
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, james-the-just, moo-james-pntc]
- **Type:** interpretive

### C-R1-010
- **Claim:** By calling readers “the twelve tribes,” James claims they constitute the true people of God of the “last days,” echoing prophetic regathering hope and Jesus’ choice of twelve apostles (Matt. 19:28; cf. Rev. 7:5–8; 21:12).
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "By calling his readers \"the twelve tribes,\" then, James claims that they constitute the true people of God of the \"last days.\""
- **Locus:** Jas 1:1 / twelve tribes (cache L17)
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **Type:** interpretive

### C-R1-011
- **Claim:** “Scattered among the nations” renders Greek “in the diaspora”; given James’s early date and Jewish audience, the term here is more literal than Peter’s figurative use—Jewish Christians dispersed through persecution (Acts 11:19).
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "The phrase \"scattered among the nations\" translates a Greek phrase meaning, literally, \"in the diaspora.\" \"Diaspora,\" or \"Dispersion\" (NRSV), became a technical name for all the nations outside of Palestine where Jewish people had come to live (2 Macc. 1:27; John 7:35). In his first letter, Peter uses this term to address his readers, who are almost certainly Gentiles (1:1). Here the word probably has a figurative meaning, characterizing Christians as people who live in this world, apart from their true, heavenly, \"homeland.\" But the early date and Jewish audience of James suggest a more literal meaning for the term here. As we argued in the Introduction, James writes to Jewish Christians who have been \"dispersed\" as a result of persecution (Acts 11:19)."
- **Locus:** Jas 1:1 / diaspora (cache L19)
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **Type:** interpretive

### C-R1-012
- **Claim:** Verses 2–18 comprise the opening section; it is not a clearly defined section with a single unifying theme, though key motifs recur—especially endurance of trials and spiritual wholeness/integrity.
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "Verses 2-18, then, comprise the opening section of the letter. But, as the diversity of opinions about the structure of the chapter reveals, it is hardly a clearly defined section. Nor does it have a unifying theme. Only by reading into the text considerably more than James says can a single topic be imposed on the section as a whole. But we can, perhaps, identify key motifs that recur in a way that suggests that they are basic to James's concern at this point. The first of these is the endurance of trials. … But perhaps even more important is the second motif: spiritual wholeness, or integrity."
- **Locus:** Jas 1:2–18 / structure and themes (cache L55)
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, double-mindedness, moo-james-pntc]
- **Type:** interpretive

### C-R1-013
- **Claim:** Greek wordplays forge literary links across chap. 1: *chairein* (v. 1) / *charan* (v. 2); *leipomenoi* (v. 4) / *leipetai* (v. 5); *peirasmon* (v. 12) / *peirazomenos* (v. 13); *teleios* in vv. 4, 17, 25.
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "Wordplays, evident in the Greek text but usually not in the English, forge literary links between many of these sections: • chairein (\"greetings\") in v. 1 is picked up by charan (\"joy\") in v. 2 • leipomenoi (\"lacking\") in v. 4b is picked up by leipetai (\"lacks\") in v. 5 • peirasmon (\"trial\") in v. 12 is picked up by peirazomenos (\"when tempted\") in v. 13 • Note also that teleios (\"perfect,\" \"complete\") occurs in vv. 4, 17, and 25"
- **Locus:** Jas 1:1–25 / literary links (cache L43–51)
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **Type:** textual-observation

### C-R1-014
- **Claim:** Spiritual wholeness is central: perseverance aims at believers “mature and complete, not lacking anything” (v. 4); the opposite is the doubter, the “double-minded man” (vv. 5–8)—a consistent and undivided commitment to God in Christ.
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "Perseverance in trials has as its ultimate outcome believers who are \"mature and complete, not lacking anything\" (v. 4). The opposite of this whole and consistent Christian is the doubter, the \"double-minded man,\" who will not find his prayers for wisdom answered (vv. 5-8). These texts portray the positive and negative side of a concern that is central to the entire letter: a consistent and undivided commitment to God in Christ."
- **Locus:** Jas 1:2–8 / spiritual wholeness (cache L55)
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, double-mindedness, moo-james-pntc]
- **Type:** interpretive

### C-R1-015
- **Claim:** Unlike most NT letters, James launches directly into exhortation after the opening, with no thanksgiving/blessing; placing trials first suggests the tough times believers faced were a key reason for writing.
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "After the initial epistolary opening, most NT letter writers express appreciation for their readers in the form of a thanksgiving or offer a blessing to God for his abundant spiritual provision. Not so James. He launches directly into exhortation. By placing trials in this position of prominence in the letter, James suggests that the tough times the believers were facing were a key reason for his writing to them."
- **Locus:** Jas 1:2 / opening of body (cache L61)
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **Type:** interpretive

### C-R1-016
- **Claim:** God brings difficulties into believers’ lives for a purpose accomplished only if they respond rightly; James gives no complete answer to undeserved suffering, but implies suffering is under the providential control of a God who wants the best for his people.
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "As do Paul (Rom. 5:2-4) and Peter (1 Pet. 1:5-7) in similar passages, James reminds his readers that God brings difficulties into believers' lives for a purpose, and that this purpose can be accomplished only if they respond in the right way to their problems. … James gives no complete answer. But implicit in what James says is a conviction that the suffering of believers is always under the providential control of a God who wants only the best for his people."
- **Locus:** Jas 1:2–4 / purpose of trials (cache L61)
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **Type:** interpretive

### C-R1-017
- **Claim:** “My brothers” is James’s favorite address (and “my dear brothers”); used spiritually it includes men and women, justifying “brothers and sisters.”
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "James's favorite address of his readers is \"my brothers\" (see also 2:1, 14; 3:1, 10, 12; 4:11; 5:7, 9-10, 12, 19) or the variant \"my dear brothers\" (1:16, 19; 2:5). Both Jews and pagans broadened the word \"brother\" to describe fellow members of the same religion … When used in this spiritual sense, the word included both men and women; hence the rendering \"brothers and sisters\" (NRSV; NLT) in modern English is justified."
- **Locus:** Jas 1:2 / address (cache L63)
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **Type:** linguistic

### C-R1-018
- **Claim:** “Pure joy” (*pasan charan*) suggests intensity—complete, unalloyed joy—not exclusivity (nothing but joy); trials should be an occasion for genuine rejoicing, not that believers never be saddened.
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "\"Pure joy\" is a good rendering of the Greek phrase pasan charan (lit., \"all joy\") since the word pas here probably suggests intensity (complete and unalloyed joy) rather than exclusivity (nothing but joy). … James does not, then, suggest that Christians facing trials will have no response other than joy, as if we were commanded never to be saddened by difficulties. His point, rather, is that trials should be an occasion for genuine rejoicing."
- **Locus:** Jas 1:2 / pure joy (cache L63)
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **Type:** linguistic / interpretive

### C-R1-019
- **Claim:** *Peirasmos* / *peirazo* can mean outward trial/testing or inner enticement to sin (“temptation”); in v. 2 the surrounding language shows “trial,” while vv. 13–15 may combine both ideas.
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "These words have two distinct meanings in the NT. They can denote either an outward trial or process of \"testing\" or they can denote the inner enticement to sin: \"temptation\" or \"tempt.\" … A combination of meanings of this kind may well be present in vv. 13-15. In v. 2, however, peirasmos means \"trial.\" The surrounding language makes this clear: believers run the risk of \"falling into\" (peripipto; translated \"face\" in NIV) these trials, which have as their purpose the \"testing\" of faith and need to be \"endured.\""
- **Locus:** Jas 1:2, 12–14 / peirasmos (cache L65)
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **Type:** linguistic / interpretive

### C-R1-020
- **Claim:** Readers’ trials prominently included poverty, partly from religious persecution by the rich (2:6–7; 5:1–6) and exile; “of many kinds” deliberately widens the net to sickness, loneliness, bereavement, disappointment, etc.
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "What were the \"trials\" that James's readers were enduring? Poverty must certainly have been prominent among them. … James 2:6-7 makes pretty clear that religious persecution was one of the causes of the poverty the believers were experiencing. … And this in turn suggests that the \"trials\" James mentions include more than religious persecution. By stressing that the trials were \"of many kinds,\" James deliberately casts his net widely, including the many kinds of suffering that Christians undergo in this fallen world: sickness, loneliness, bereavement, disappointment."
- **Locus:** Jas 1:2 / kinds of trials (cache L67)
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **Type:** historical / interpretive

### C-R1-021
- **Claim:** “Testing” (*dokimion*) denotes the process of refining (as silver/gold in LXX), not merely determining whether faith exists; difficulties refine existing faith so impurities are removed.
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "\"Testing\" translates a rare Greek word (dokimion), which is found elsewhere in the NT only in 1 Pet. 1:7 and in the Septuagint only in Ps. 11:7 (ET 12:6) and Prov. 27:21. … the two OT occurrences both denote the process of refining silver or gold, and this is the way James uses the word. The difficulties of life are intended by God to refine our faith: heating it in the crucible of suffering so that impurities might be refined away and so that it might become pure and valuable before the Lord. The \"testing of faith\" here, then, is not intended to determine whether a person has faith or not; it is intended to purify faith that already exists."
- **Locus:** Jas 1:3 / testing of faith (cache L69)
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **Type:** linguistic / interpretive

### C-R1-022
- **Claim:** Testing produces perseverance (*hypomonē*): “remaining under,” like carrying a heavy load long; trials produce endurance as a muscle strengthens under resistance (Trench: *hypomonē* vs *makrothymia*, though James later uses *makrothymeō* for both senses).
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "Testing produces, first of all, perseverance. The etymology of the Greek word points to the idea of \"remaining under,\" and, in this case, etymology steers us in the right direction. The picture is of a person successfully carrying a heavy load for a long time. … Like a muscle that becomes strong when it faces resistance, so Christians learn to remain faithful to God over the long haul only when they face difficulty."
- **Locus:** Jas 1:3 / perseverance (cache L71)
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **Type:** linguistic / interpretive

### C-R1-023
- **Claim:** Believers must “let endurance have its perfect work”; benefits come only with right response. The “perfect work” is not merely full extent of perseverance itself but the many dimensions of ideal Christian character.
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "believers should \"let endurance have its perfect [or complete] work.\" … the benefits of testing come only to believers who respond to them in the right way: Christians must allow endurance to do its intended work. … But James's deep concern throughout the letter that believers respond to God's grace with sincere obedience suggests rather that the word \"work\" here summarizes the many dimensions of the ideal Christian character."
- **Locus:** Jas 1:4 / perfect work of perseverance (cache L73)
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **Type:** interpretive

### C-R1-024
- **Claim:** *Teleios* in Greek moral philosophy often means “perfect”; in OT/Jewish background “complete/mature” (e.g. Noah). Moo argues against lowering the bar: nothing less than complete moral integrity will ultimately satisfy holy God; “complete” suggests wholeness/soundness—spiritual integrity at the heart of James’s concern (esp. 1:7–8; 4:4–5).
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "In Greek moral philosophy, this word usually had the meaning \"perfect.\" But in the OT and in Jewish literature, teleios is colored by its Hebrew background and comes to mean \"complete\" or \"mature.\" … But we should not \"lower the bar\" on the expectation James sets for us. Nothing less than complete moral integrity will ultimately satisfy the God who is himself holy and righteous, completely set apart from sin. … Testing, James suggests, is intended to produce, when believers respond with confidence in God and determination to endure, a wholeness of Christian character that lacks nothing in the panoply of virtues that define Godly character. This concern for spiritual integrity and wholeness lies at the heart of James's concern, and he will come back to the matter again and again (see esp. 1:7-8 and 4:4-5)."
- **Locus:** Jas 1:4 / teleios / wholeness (cache L73–75)
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, double-mindedness, moo-james-pntc]
- **Type:** linguistic / interpretive

### C-R1-025
- **Claim:** Vv. 5–8 connect via “lack” (v. 4b/5a); spiritual perfection as goal of trials is achieved only when divine wisdom is present, available for sincere asking—Jewish wisdom links testing, wisdom, and integrity (e.g. Sir. 4:17; Wis. 9:6; 10:5) likely influence sequence.
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "James uses a verbal link to connect these two brief paragraphs, with the word lack ending the former (v. 4b) and introducing the latter (v. 5a). … The spiritual perfection that is the goal of trials (vv. 2-4) will be achieved only when divine wisdom is present. And wisdom can be had for the asking - albeit, an asking that is sincere and uncorrupted (vv. 6-8)."
- **Locus:** Jas 1:5–8 / wisdom after trials (cache L81)
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **Type:** interpretive

### C-R1-026
- **Claim:** James’s view of wisdom stays in the practical tradition of Proverbs, Wisdom of Solomon, and Sirach; he shows no interest in metaphysical “lady wisdom” speculation.
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "But James betrays no interest in these more metaphysical speculations. His view of wisdom remains solidly in the practical tradition of Proverbs, the Wisdom of Solomon, and Sirach."
- **Locus:** Jas 1:5 / wisdom (cache L83)
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **Type:** interpretive

### C-R1-027
- **Claim:** “He should ask God… and it will be given” intentionally echoes Jesus’ “Ask and it will be given to you” (Matt. 7:7a); God gives because he gives generously / with character that grounds prayer.
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "It is therefore more than likely that the combination of exhortation and promise in the second part of v. 5 - he should ask God, who gives generously to all without finding fault, and it will be given to him - is an intentional echo of Jesus' pithier \"Ask and it will be given to you\" (Matt. 7:7a)."
- **Locus:** Jas 1:5 / ask God (cache L85)
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **Type:** interpretive

### C-R1-028
- **Claim:** Against dominant “generously,” Moo argues the hapax adverb from the “single/simple” root more likely stresses God’s single, undivided intent to give needed gifts—fitting James’s integrity theme and “without finding fault” (contrast Sir. 20:14–15).
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "Taken together, then, the evidence suggests that James is not so much highlighting God's generosity in giving as his single, undivided intent to give us those gifts we need to please him.19 The negative qualification to God's giving, \"without finding fault,\" also fits this interpretation. According to Sirach, \"a fool's gift will profit you nothing, for he has many eyes instead of one. He gives little and upbraids (oneidizei) much\" (20:14-15a). In contrast, James portrays God as one who gives \"simply,\" \"with one eye,\" and without finding fault (oneidizontos)."
- **Locus:** Jas 1:5 / haplōs / without finding fault (cache L89–91)
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, double-mindedness, moo-james-pntc]
- **Type:** linguistic / interpretive

### C-R1-029
- **Claim:** Asking must match God’s singleness of intent: believe and not doubt; teaching applies to prayer generally (parallels elsewhere), not wisdom only; not a health-and-wealth blank check—qualified by what God has promised (here wisdom, v. 5).
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "Indeed, our asking must coincide with the way in which God gives: he gives with singleness of intent; we must ask with singleness of intent. Specifically, James calls on us to believe and not doubt as we come to God in prayer. … So we are probably justified in taking his teaching in these verses to apply to any prayer. … But neither Jesus nor James intends to give to Christians a blank check on which they can write whatever they want and expect God to back it up. The \"whatever you ask\" is clearly qualified by Scripture elsewhere to include only what God has promised to give his people (see, further, our comments on 5:14). In James this point is clear from the connection with v. 5, where he speaks first of God's desire to give wisdom to his people."
- **Locus:** Jas 1:5–6 / faith in prayer (cache L95–97)
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **Type:** interpretive

### C-R1-030
- **Claim:** “Doubt” (middle of *diakrinō*) is strong: basic division within the believer causing wavering; not that any degree of doubt voids prayer (Abraham’s consistency over years, Rom. 4:20), but God responds when life reflects basic consistency of purpose—spiritual integrity.
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "But as the word's basic meaning suggests, James is probably thinking of a strong kind of doubting: a basic division within the believer that brings about wavering and inconsistency of attitude toward God. … James is not, then, here claiming that prayers will never be answered where any degree of doubt exists - for some degree of doubt on at least some occasions is probably inevitable in our present state of weakness. Rather, he wants us to understand that God responds to us only when our lives reflect a basic consistency of purpose and intent: a spiritual integrity."
- **Locus:** Jas 1:6 / doubt (cache L97)
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, double-mindedness, moo-james-pntc]
- **Type:** linguistic / interpretive

### C-R1-031
- **Claim:** The doubter is like a sea swell, constantly changing with wind (not a crashing wave); without anchor, prey to shifting motives—wanting God’s wisdom one day and the world’s the next.
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "At the end of v. 6, James compares the person who doubts to a wave of the sea, blown and tossed by the wind. The picture here is not of a wave mounting in height and crashing to shore, but of the swell of the sea, never having the same texture and shape from moment to moment, but always changing with the variations in wind direction and strength. … So the doubter, not possessing an \"anchor for the soul\" (Heb. 6:19), does not pray to God with a consistency and sincerity of purpose. Prey to the shifting winds of motive and desire, he wants wisdom from God one day and the wisdom of the world the next."
- **Locus:** Jas 1:6 / wave of the sea (cache L99–103)
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, double-mindedness, moo-james-pntc]
- **Type:** interpretive

### C-R1-032
- **Claim:** *Dipsychos* (“double-souled”) first appears here in Greek literature; James likely coined it (again at 4:8) to accentuate wholehearted, consistent faith; concept has OT precedents (whole/divided heart; Deut. 6:5; Sir. 2:12 “two ways”).
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "The Greek word for doubleminded is dipsychos, which is literally translated \"double-souled.\" This is the first time in Greek literature that this particular word occurs.25 James, who uses this same word again in 4:8, has probably coined the term in order to accentuate his concern that believers display a wholehearted, consistent, and integral faith commitment to God. However, while he may be the first to use this particular word, he is certainly not the first to enunci ate the concept. The OT blesses those who pursue God with \"a whole heart\" (Ps. 119:2) and condemns the person who exhibits a \"divided heart\" (Ps. 12:2; Hos. 10:2)."
- **Locus:** Jas 1:8 / dipsychos (cache L115)
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, double-mindedness, moo-james-pntc]
- **Type:** linguistic / interpretive

### C-R1-033
- **Claim:** “Unstable in all he does” portrays basic inconsistency of attitude, not occasional lapse—“spiritual schizophrenia”: a basic division in the soul that contradicts one’s claim to belong to God.
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "The \"all he does\" reflects again James's concern to portray a basic inconsistency in attitude and spirit rather than an occasional doubt or lapse. It is what we might call \"spiritual schizophrenia\" that James criticizes in these verses explicitly and implicitly throughout his letter: a basic division in the soul that leads to thinking, speaking, and acting that contradicts one's claim to belong to God."
- **Locus:** Jas 1:7–8 / unstable (cache L117)
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, double-mindedness, moo-james-pntc]
- **Type:** interpretive

### C-R1-034
- **Claim:** Vv. 9–11 contrast “brother in humble circumstances” and “one who is rich,” each to “take pride” in high vs low position; identity of the rich person is contested—Christian vs non-Christian—and Moo keeps options open through the exegesis.
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "The heart of the paragraph is a contrast between a \"brother in humble circumstances\" and \"one who is rich.\" Each is exhorted by James to \"take pride\" or \"boast\": the humble brother in his \"high position\" and the rich person in his \"low position.\" What makes the interpretation difficult and contentious is the problem of identifying the \"one who is rich.\"27 About half the commentators on James think that this rich person is a Christian. … The other view, equally supported in the literature, is that the rich person is a non-Christian."
- **Locus:** Jas 1:9–11 / poor and rich identity (cache L123)
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **Type:** interpretive-crux

### C-R1-035
- **Claim:** “Humble” here is socioeconomic (contrast “rich”), drawing on LXX lowly/poor tradition and reversal (Luke 1:52); if readers left Jerusalem for Syria/N. Palestine, most face tough finances and social dislocation.
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "Since the contrast in this context is between \"humble\" and \"rich\" (v. 10), James is clearly using the word to describe the believer's socioeconomic situation. If, as we think, the Christians to whom James writes have been forced to leave Jerusalem and establish new homes in Syria and northern Palestine, most of them would be facing tough financial situations as well as social dislocation and even ostracism."
- **Locus:** Jas 1:9 / humble circumstances (cache L125)
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **Type:** interpretive

### C-R1-036
- **Claim:** “Take pride” is not always wrong (Jer. 9:23–24); the humble brother should boast in exaltation—heavenly status, already belonging by faith; God has chosen the poor to be rich in faith (Jas. 2:5).
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "From this text it becomes clear that \"boasting\" is not in itself always wrong; it is a matter of what it is that one is boasting in, or taking pride in. Christians, however difficult their circumstances in this world, can always take pride in their \"high position,\" or \"exaltation.\" … James's point, then, is that believers must look beyond the world's evaluation to understand who they are and look to God's view of them. And he has \"chosen those who are poor in the eyes of the world to be rich in faith and to inherit the kingdom he promised to those who love him\" (Jas. 2:5)."
- **Locus:** Jas 1:9 / high position (cache L129–131)
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **Type:** interpretive

### C-R1-037
- **Claim:** On balance Moo prefers both rich and poor as Christians: poor take pride in exalted spiritual status; rich take pride, paradoxically, in humble identification with the despised Christ—evaluate by spiritual not material standards (countercultural church).
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "While the evidence does not all point in the same direction, we think that the balance shifts toward the view that James in these verses addresses two Christians, a poor one and a rich one. He exhorts each of them to look toward their spiritual identity as the measure of their ultimate significance. … To the rich believer, tempted to think too much of himself because the world holds him in high esteem, James says: take pride not in your money or in your social position - things that are doomed all too soon to fade away forever - but, paradoxically, in your humble status as a person who identifies with one who was \"despised and rejected\" by the world. The point of the passage is, then, that Christians must always evaluate themselves by spiritual and not material standards."
- **Locus:** Jas 1:9–11 / conclusion on rich Christian (cache L143)
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **Type:** interpretive

### C-R1-038
- **Claim:** Transitoriness of wealth is imaged by wild flower/vegetation (Isa. 40:6b–8; Ps. 103:15–16; 49:16–17); sun’s scorching heat or scorching wind withers plant; rich fade even while about business—“pass away” typically “cease to exist,” not clearly judgment language.
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "James backs up his warning to the rich person with a reminder of the transitoriness of all human wealth and status. The annual death of vegetation provides a natural metaphor for this purpose, and James draws on a rich biblical tradition when he uses it here. … And so, James asserts, the rich person will pass away like a wild flower. … the verb \"pass away\" is never used in the NT to denote judgment. Rather, it typically has the idea \"cease to exist\" … In the same way, James asserts, the rich man will fade away even while he goes about his business."
- **Locus:** Jas 1:10–11 / flower of the field (cache L139–141)
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **Type:** interpretive

### C-R1-039
- **Claim:** Contextually, poverty/wealth may be a (or the) greatest “test,” and/or money is a chief threat to double-souled compromise of wholehearted commitment (Matt. 6:24).
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "So James may intend us to see poverty and wealth as a, or perhaps even the, greatest \"test\" for Christians.34 But these verses might also be tied to James's overriding concern throughout this section: that Christians display a consistent and integral spirituality that avoids the \"double-souled\" attitude typical of too many who claim to be followers of Christ. Money and the things that money can buy, James well knows, are a tremendously powerful lure to compromise one's wholehearted commitment to the Lord."
- **Locus:** Jas 1:9–11 in context of 1:2–8 (cache L145)
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, double-mindedness, moo-james-pntc]
- **Type:** interpretive

### C-R1-040
- **Claim:** V. 12 returns to trials via verbal links (*peirasmos*, persevere/perseverance, test/testing); promises reward for successful endurance. “Blessed” should not be reduced to “happy”; favor may coexist with varying emotions.
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "With this verse, James returns to the opening topic of the paragraph: trials. Verbal similarities reveal the connection. \"Trial\" occurs in both vv. 2 and 12; the verb \"persevere\" in v. 12 picks up \"perseverance\" in vv. 3-4; and \"test\" in v. 12 matches the \"testing\" of v. 3. … The tendency to translate with the word \"happy\" (e.g., TEV, REB) is a misguided effort to avoid unclear \"religious\" language and should be resisted. A person who is \"blessed\" may not be \"happy\" at all."
- **Locus:** Jas 1:12 / blessed endurance (cache L151)
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **Type:** interpretive

### C-R1-041
- **Claim:** “Crown of life” uses athletic laurel-wreath imagery of reward (cf. 1 Cor. 9:25; Rev. 2:10); *life* indicates what the reward is; God promised it to those who love him—no single specific OT promise need be pinned down. Contemplating reward spurs faithfulness without reducing service to selfish calculation.
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "Christians who stand up under the test will receive the crown of life that God has promised to those who love him. The word crown conveys to most of us a gem-studded headpiece worn by kings and queens. But people in the Greco-Roman world would probably have thought more often of the laurel wreath given to the victors in athletic contests. … If James, then, uses the crown to refer to the idea of reward, then the word life following crown will indicate what the reward is.36 Revelation 2:10, a word of Jesus to suffering Christians, is similar: \"Be faithful, even to the point of death, and I will give you the crown of life.\" … Clearly James's overall purpose in this verse is to encourage believ ers to endure trials faithfully so that we might receive the reward that God has promised. … But the contemplation of heaven's rewards is found throughout the NT as a spur to our faithfulness in difficult circumstances here on earth."
- **Locus:** Jas 1:12 / crown of life (cache L153–155)
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **Type:** interpretive

### C-R1-042
- **Claim:** V. 12 is hinge between 2–11 and 13–18: inclusio with 2–4, yet *peirazo* links to temptation in 13–14; every trial carries temptation—God may bring/allow trials but is not author of temptation.
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "Verse 12 is the hinge between vv. 2-11 and vv. 13-18. … As the verbal resemblances we pointed out above reveal, vv. 2-4 and v. 12 appear to form just such an inclusio. But v. 12 has obvious connections with vv. 13-15 as well. The Greek word for \"test\" in v. 12, peirazo, is the same word that is translated \"tempt\" in vv. 13-14. Using this term as a link-word, therefore, James makes the transition from testing to temptation. God, James has said, promises a blessing to those who endure trials. Every trial, every external difficulty, carries with it a temptation, an inner enticement to sin. God may bring, or allow, trials; but he is not, James insists, the author of temptation (v. 13)."
- **Locus:** Jas 1:12–13 / test → tempt (cache L161)
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **Type:** interpretive

### C-R1-043
- **Claim:** No solid line between testing and temptation: financial difficulty can tempt questioning providence; death of loved one, God’s love; suffering of righteous poor vs ease of wicked rich, God’s justice or existence. OT shows God tests (Abraham, Israel, Hezekiah) but never seeks to induce sin and destroy faith—must distinguish outer trial and inner temptation despite same Greek root.
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "No solid line should be drawn between v. 12 and v. 13, as if James drops the topic of testing to take up the issue of temptation. His concern, rather, is to help his readers resist the temptation that comes along with the trial. For every trial brings temptation. Financial difficulty can tempt us to question God's providence in our lives. The death of a loved one can tempt us to question God's love for us. The suffering of the righteous poor and the ease of the wicked rich can tempt us to question God's justice, or even his existence. … But while God may test or prove his servants in order to strengthen their faith, he never seeks to induce sin and destroy their faith. Thus, despite the fact that the same Greek root (peira-) is used for both the outer trial and the inner temptation, it is crucial to distinguish them."
- **Locus:** Jas 1:12–13 / God tests but does not tempt (cache L167)
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **Type:** interpretive

### C-R1-044
- **Claim:** Traditional rendering preferred: God cannot be tempted by evil (*apeirastos* passive “unable to be tempted”), and therefore tempts no one—play on *peirazo*; Hort “inexperienced” and Davids “ought not to be tested” rejected.
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "Thus James insists that God cannot be tempted by evil. This rendering, which is paralleled in most English translations, understands the rare word apeirastos as a passive verbal adjective with the meaning \"unable to be tempted.\" But two other possibilities should be mentioned. … Neither alternative is preferable to the traditional interpretation. … If we adopt the NIV rendering, then, how does the clause contribute to James's argument? Presumably, it is to be seen as a preliminary observation leading on to the main point: he himself tempts no one. \"What must be understood is that temptation is an impulse to sin, and since God is not susceptible to any such desire for evil he cannot be seen as desiring that it be brought about in man.\"44"
- **Locus:** Jas 1:13 / apeirastos (cache L169)
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **Type:** linguistic / interpretive

### C-R1-045
- **Claim:** Temptation is attributed to each one’s own evil desire (*epithymia*—fleshly illicit desire, broader than sexual); responsibility on the human person; omission of Satan here does not deny him (cf. 4:7) but highlights individual responsibility; fishing metaphor (dragged away/enticed) may be a “dead” metaphor by James’s day.
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "James now attributes temptation to each person's evil desire. No Greek word corresponding to \"evil\" is found in the text, but the NIV rendering is nevertheless justified. \"Desire\" (epithyniia) can have a neutral meaning in the NT … but the context here makes it clear that James uses it with its more typical NT sense: fleshly, illicit desire. … The most we can say is that James, like other Jewish and Christian authors, wants to place the responsibility for temptation and sin squarely on the shoulders of each human being. Nor should we make anything of James's omission of Satan as a source of temptation. James refers to Satan elsewhere (4:7). But his purpose here is to highlight individual responsibility for sin."
- **Locus:** Jas 1:14 / desire (cache L171)
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **Type:** interpretive

### C-R1-046
- **Claim:** Desire conceives and gives birth to sin; full-grown sin gives birth to death. Temptation itself is not sin—only when desire is welcomed and “conceives” does sin come into being; maturity is infrequency of *succumbing*, not of temptation (cf. Heb. 2:18). Imagery recalls Proverbs’ “loose woman” vs wisdom (life vs death).
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "Aided by the fact that the underlying Greek word is feminine, James pictures desire as conceiving and giving birth to sin. And sin, once in existence, if it becomes full-grown, produces death. … James implies that temptation, in and of itself, is not sinful. Only when desire \"conceives\" - is allowed to produce offspring - does sin come into being. … Christian maturity is not indicated by the infrequency of temptation but by the infrequency of succumbing to temptation. … the image of \"desire\" as a seductress luring the believer into an adulterous union that brings death is reminiscent of the role played by the \"loose woman\" in Proverbs 5-9."
- **Locus:** Jas 1:15 / desire → sin → death (cache L175)
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **Type:** interpretive

### C-R1-047
- **Claim:** “Don’t be deceived, my dear brothers” (v. 16) is transitional—opening what follows about God as source of good gifts, and looking back to the source of temptation (vv. 13–15).
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "James therefore does not want his readers to make any mistake about what he is about to say about God as the source of all good gifts. But the warning also refers back to the reminder about the source of temptation in vv. 1315. It therefore serves as a transition between vv. 13-15 and vv. 17-18.48 Believers, James is saying, must not be led astray into thinking that God himself is tempting them to evil; on the contrary, he is the invariable giver of good gifts to his children."
- **Locus:** Jas 1:16 / transition (cache L179)
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **Type:** interpretive

### C-R1-048
- **Claim:** Vv. 17–18 conclude 2–18: return to God’s singleness/integrity in giving (v. 5); contrast with 13–15 (God gives good, does not tempt to evil); “word” introduces theme of 19–27. Greek “every good giving and every perfect gift” is imperfect hexameter—repetition for style, not two meanings; *teleios* inclusio with v. 4.
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "As the conclusion to this unit, vv. 17-18 serve several purposes. First, they bring us back to the theme of the singleness and integrity of God, especially in his giving (see v. 5). Second, as we have noted, this theme in turn provides a contrast with vv. 13-15: God does not tempt to evil; he gives good gifts. And, third, the mention of the \"word\" (of God) in v. 18 introduces the theme that will dominate vv. 19-27. … The words of the Greek text here form an imperfect hexameter. The repetition of the \"giving\" idea, then, is necessary in order to create this literary form, and no difference in meaning between the two Greek words should be seen.50 The same is probably true of the adjectives \"good\" and \"perfect,\" although the latter word (Gk. teleios) touches on a key motif in James and creates something of an inclusio with the same word in v. 4."
- **Locus:** Jas 1:17–18 / good and perfect gift (cache L181–183)
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **Type:** interpretive / literary

### C-R1-049
- **Claim:** Good gifts come “from above,” from “the Father of the heavenly lights” (sun, moon, stars)—creation language for God’s power and care. God “does not change like shifting shadows”: preferred text “variation or shadow of turning”; astronomical imagery contrasts unchangeable God with constantly moving heavens—integrity/undividedness of God vs human duality (vv. 7–8), key motif of the letter.
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "every good and perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of the heavenly lights. … James, therefore, cites God's creation of the heavenly bodies as evidence of his power and continuing care for the world. … James is not writing a scientific treatise but is using general language about the constant motion of the heavenly bodies to make a point about God: he does not change like the heavens do. … Indeed, the integrity and undividedness of God - in contrast to the duality and instability of man (cf. vv. 7-8) - is a key motif of the letter as a whole."
- **Locus:** Jas 1:17 / Father of lights; no variation (cache L187–189)
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, double-mindedness, moo-james-pntc]
- **Type:** interpretive

### C-R1-050
- **Claim:** Birth “through the word of truth” is preferably redemptive new birth, not mere creation: “word of truth” elsewhere = gospel as saving agent; links to logos in 1:21–23 able to “save your souls”; *bouletheis* stresses free choice; believers as “firstfruits” of a redemptive plan eventually encompassing all creation.
- **Attribution:** Moo
- **Quote:** "But the most important piece of evidence in favor of a redemptive \"birth\" here is the phrase \"the word of truth.\" The syntax suggests that this \"word\" is the instrument through which God brings people to life. All four of the other occurrences of the phrase in the NT refer to the gospel as the agent of salvation (2 Cor. 6:7; Eph. 1:13; Col. 1:5; 2 Tim. 2:15). … But we think the phrase \"word of truth,\" coupled with the allusion to this same word as able to \"save your souls\" in v. 21, tips the scales in favor of the redemptive interpretation. James, therefore, appeals to the \"new birth\" of Christians as a striking example of God's good and faithful giving. James stresses the free and unconstrained nature of this giving by beginning the verses with the participle \"willing\" (bouletheis) … God's grace has been extended through the gospel to people so as to bring into existence a foretaste, or down payment (\"firstfruits\"), of a redemptive plan that will eventually encompass all of creation."
- **Locus:** Jas 1:18 / word of truth; firstfruits (cache L191–193)
- **Tags:** [james, douglas-moo, moo-james-pntc]
- **Type:** interpretive
